notes.text: Depths — Deep wells or springs, or lakes, which were numerous and large.
Whose stones are iron — Where are mines of iron in a manner as plentiful as stones, and upon which travelers must tread, as in other parts they do upon stones.

Bless the Lord — Solemnly praise him for thy food; which is a debt both of gratitude and justice, because it is from his providence and favour that thou receivest both thy food and refreshment and strength by it. The more unworthy and absurd is that too common profaneness of them, who, professing to believe a God, from whom all their comforts come, grudge to own him at their meals, either by desiring his blessing before them, or by offering due praise to God after them.
Lifted up — As if thou didst receive and enjoy these things, either, by thy owns wisdom, and valour, and industry, or for thy own merit.

That he might humble thee — By keeping thee in a constant dependence upon him for every day's food, and convincing thee what an impotent, helpless creature thou art, having nothing whereon to subsist, and being supported wholly by the alms of divine goodness from day to day. The mercies of God, if duly considered, are as powerful a mean to humble us as the greatest afflictions, because they increase our debts to God, and manifest our dependance upon him, and by making God great, they make us little in our own eyes. To do thee good - That is, that after he hath purged and prepared thee by afflictions, thou mayest receive and enjoy his blessings with less disadvantage, whilst by the remembrance of former afflictions. thou art made thankful for them, and more cautious not to abuse them. A promise of Canaan, ver. 1-3. A caution, not to ascribe this to their own merit, ver. 4-6. A rehearsal of their various rebellions, ver. 7-24. and of Moses's intercession for them, ver. 25-29.

glossa.text:
*Judgments.* Those which were enjoined upon the people by Moses at divers times after the law was given, which in Exodus are called justifications.

*And ceremonies.* Circumcision, the rites of sacrifices. Whence Ambrose on the *Epistle to the Romans*: Threefold (says he) is the law: the first part is of the sacrament of the Godhead; the second agrees with the natural law, which forbids sin; the third is of the feasts of the law, that is, sabbaths, new moons, and circumcision.

*And the dipsas.* A kind of asp which in Latin is called *situla*: whomsoever it has bitten perishes of thirst; so small that when it is trodden upon it is not seen. Its venom extinguishes before it is felt, nor does he who is to die feel any sadness.

Mystically. The divers serpents are heresies, differing indeed among themselves, but all deadly.

notes.text: Approach — To draw near to God in his house and ordinance, by prayer and praise, and other acts of communion with him. Satisfied - With the blessings there conferred upon thy people, the favour and fellowship of God, remission of sins, renovation of heart and life, joy and peace, and well-grounded assurance of eternal life.

Righteousness — By virtue of thy faithfulness, and goodness. Wilt thou - Thou wilt graciously answer our prayers. The confidence - Thou art the stay and support of all mankind, by thy powerful and gracious providence.
Tumult — No less wild and impetuous.

Thy tokens — Terrible thunders and lightnings, and earthquakes, and comets or other strange meteors, or works of God in the air. Morning - The successive courses of the morning and evening; or of the sun and moon which go forth at those times. Thus the whole verse speaks of the natural works of God, the former clause, of such as are extraordinary and terrible, the latter of such as are ordinary and delightful.

River — With rain, which he very significantly calls a river for its plenty, and the river of God, of God's immediate providing. Them - The inhabitants of the earth. Provided - Or, disposed, the earth, which without this would be hard and barren.
Bringest down — For the rain dissolves the high and hard clods of earth.
Wilderness — Which though neglected by men, are furnished with food for beasts.

Sing — They are abundantly satisfied with thy goodness, and in their manner sing forth the praise of their benefactor. The psalmist calls on all people to praise God, for his sovereign power over the whole creation, ver. 1-7. For his special favour to his people, ver. 8-12. Praises him for his goodness to himself in particular, ver. 13-20. To the chief musician, A song or psalm.

glossa.text: *It becometh thee.* Not the gods of the nations, and not elsewhere, save in contemplation, that is, in faith, and there out of good works *the vow shall be paid,* in the heavenly Jerusalem, the vow which those men used to pay to Mars after battles, and to the other gods in this fashion. *Sion.* Sion is the heavenly country, the same is Jerusalem.

*Hear my prayer.* ((CASS.)) He first does what he says is to be done by the rest, namely, *hear. All flesh.* ((AUG.)) That is, man, that is, out of every kind: poor, rich, men, women, learned, unlearned, boys, old men.

*The words of the wicked.* ((CASS.)) In what hope dost thou pray this? Because *to thee all flesh shall come,* not the soul only, but the evil man also. It is necessary that thou hear. For the words of the wicked are the words of the devil and of our first parents Adam and Eve. *They have prevailed.* That is, they cast us into exile, or the pagans persuaded their own rites to their sons, but thou wilt be merciful in the sacrifice of Christ. ((AUG.)) *The words of the wicked,* that is, we have followed the evil rites and manners of our parents (who, as in age, so in authority, surpass boys). *Thou wilt be merciful.* ((AUG.)) Propitiation is made through the sacrifice which the priest offered, Christ. The priest and the victim are therefore the same.

*Blessed is he whom thou hast chosen,* etc. ((CASS.)) And blessed is every man whom thou hast chosen out of the mass of the lost. *You have not chosen me, but I you ((Joan. XV))*, and thou hast taken him into thy lot, into eternal rest. ((AUG.)) Or thus, thou wilt be merciful through the blessed man: etc., *as far as* things which cannot be told. *In the good things.* ((CASS.)) Which things are good, holiness in oneself, equity toward one's neighbour. *The temple.* The Church, or the flesh of Christ.

*Wonderful.* ((AUG.)) Not in outward things, like a house of earth, but in justice, which is fairer to the inward eye and more lovely, and which we ought now to hunger for, that then we may be filled with it. *In equity.* ((CAS.)) When he shall render to each what is worthy, to whom [each] shall also say: *Hear us, thou who art the Saviour. The hope of all.* He describes the praises of God, and his powers. *And in the sea afar off.* ((AUG.)) Therefore afar off, because in the sea. The sea is spoken of as a figure of the world, bitter with the falsehood of iniquities, and stormy with the tempests of temptations, where the fishes devour one another.

*Preparing the mountains.* ((AUG.)) For fitting uses. *In thy strength.* Because through them he wrought miracles. How did he prepare them? Girded with power, that is, with Deity, because the humanity of the Word is girded about with majesty, so that what the man had not, the Deity might give. *Girded. ((Ibid.))* Christ in the midst, girded on every side, because we all alike have him who believe in him, but because faith is not from us, but from him, he is said to be girded with his own might.

*Who troublest the depth of the sea.* Behold, he who through those prepared ones wrought it, troubling them unto penitence. The depth of the sea, not the surface, but hearts more deeply sunk, or the hearts of princes. These were troubled, when they saw both their gods and their hopes come to nothing. *The noise.* ((AUG.)) Sounding with contradiction, tossing with persecution, etc., *as far as* while they perceive that these prevail more than their own gods.

*The morning and the evening.* ((AUG.)) The morning is prosperity, because the morning is glad after the sadness of the night. The evening is adversity; in these a man is tempted, but it is granted him to go out thence, lest he be caught by gains, he to whom riches are God: lest he be terrified by adversities, he for whom the Lord suffered. *Thou wilt delight.* Thou wilt make them delightful even in this life. For if the going out itself does not delight a man, he does not labour to go out thence, but is caught by gains, he to whom the promise of Christ is not pleasing. And he is terrified by adversities, whom he does not delight who was willing to suffer for him, that he might make a going out for him.

*Thou hast visited the earth and hast inebriated it.* Through preachers wilt thou do this, for within thou teachest those to whom they preach.

*A river.* Of the deep, for the receiving, it is filled with waters, with the gifts of the Holy Ghost, for thou hast prepared food. *The river of God.* ((CAS.)) The mercy of God is compared to a river in full flood, etc., *as far as* as it is disposed by him, without whom nothing is done there.

*Its streams.* The Apostles and others, who drank of the river. *Inebriate them,* that they may suffice for themselves and for others. *Multiply,* that through successions preaching may not fail. *The crown of the year,* the whole world, where the Church is. *Its streams. ((Ibid.)) Thou hast prepared,* etc. And, O Lord, etc., *as far as* whereby the Word of God grows. *The crown of the year. ((Ibid.))* Because the glory of victory belongs to him who conquers the devil. *Of thy bounty,* etc. ((AUG.)) Let no one glory in his own merits.

*Thy fields shall be filled.* ((CASS., AUG.)) Men, because of their evenness, that is, the just. *The hills,* because God raises up the humble *The desert:* all the Gentiles, to whom no prophet was sent.
*The beautiful places of the wilderness shall grow fat.* When the Apostles came to them, through whom they were made comely.

*Valleys. ((Ibid.))* Lowly peoples shall bring forth much fruit. *They shall cry out. ((Ibid.))* *Clamabuut* Not in blasphemy, but in a hymn, thence they abound with corn.

This psalm is sung at the funerals of the faithful, because it treats of the return from the Babylon of this world to the heavenly country, to which the saints, led forth from the flesh at their death, happily pass over, receiving the single robe, until in the resurrection they be glorified with the robe of a twofold beatitude.

notes.text: He that soweth sparingly shall reap sparingly; he that soweth bountifully shall reap bountifully — A general rule. God will proportion the reward to the work, and the temper whence it proceeds.
Of necessity — Because he cannot tell how to refuse.

How remarkable are these words! Each is loaded with matter and increases all the way it goes. All grace — Every kind of blessing. That ye may abound to every good work - God gives us everything, that we may do good therewith, and so receive more blessings. All things in this life, even rewards, are, to the faithful, seeds in order to a future harvest. Prov. xxii, 9

He hath scattered abroad — (A generous word.) With a full hand, without any anxious thought which way each grain falls. His righteousness - His beneficence, with the blessed effects of it. Remaineth forever - Unexhausted, God still renewing his store. Psalm cxii, 9

And he who supplieth seed — Opportunity and ability to help others. And bread - All things needful for your own souls and bodies. Will continually supply you with that seed, yea, multiply it to you more and more. And increase the fruits of your righteousness - The happy effects of your love to God and man. Isaiah lv, 10
Which worketh by us thanksgiving to God — Both from us who distribute, and them who receive, your bounty.
Your avowed subjection — Openly testified by your actions. To all men - Who stand in need of it.
His unspeakable gift — His outward and inward blessings, the number and excellence of which cannot be uttered.

glossa.text: *He that soweth sparingly.* He does not sow sparingly who, having little, bestows little, if his mind be ready to give more, if he had more.

*Not out of sadness.* He who gives unwillingly because of present shame has not a reward. *For a cheerful giver,* he who gives that he may be rid of the tedium of the one importuning him, not that he may refresh the bowels of the needy, loses both the merit and the thing. He gives largely who has the affection of giving largely, even if he have nothing that he can give.

*To abound,* etc. For although what he who has little bestows be scanty, yet it abounds, because it is done with right judgment: because the question is not out of how much, but with what mind, it is given.
*For justice.* He is just who reckons the goods of the world common, with a view to the end of the eternal reward.

*The increase of the fruits.* Justice is holiness, and a good life: and thence the fruits, that is, the eternal recompense. The increases of alms: for which both here virtues, and in the time to come glory, shall be increased.
*Which worketh.* That is, the bounty itself is the cause why thanks are given to God, of which bounty we are the ministers.

*Thanks be to God.* He gives thanks to God for the alternate need, and for the alternate supplying of the need, of Christ's provincials and of Christ's soldiers. He has treated here of carnal things toward those, and after he had treated of spiritual things toward these, as one full of joys he exclaims: *I give thanks,* etc.
*And it came to pass.* After the parable by which he invites to kindness and to perseverance in the diverse offices of God, the ungrateful are reproved concerning benefits bestowed.

*There met him,* etc. The lepers are heretics, who, having as it were various colours in the same body, mingle various sects, now of falsehood, now of truth, in the same preaching. But because these are shunned and removed far from the Church, they must needs cry out with a great clamour.

*Who stood,* etc. They who have sinned against the Decalogue, loving neither God (of whom they think ill) nor the neighbour, from whom they are divided, cry under the number ten to God and are healed, while in the fellowship of the Church they attain a whole and true teaching, and expound all things according to the rule of the Catholic faith, and are free of the variety of lies as of leprosy. But one gives thanks, that is, they who remain in the unity of the Church through humility; but they who, puffed up through pride, are ungrateful to him who cleansed them, are nine, because by one unit they fall short of the perfection of the number ten.

*And they lifted up their voice.* Because they acknowledge that they have erred in the words of the Saviour, they call upon the master who is to save them, and through the knowledge of the master they return to the form of salvation.

*Go,* etc. Whoever, cleansed by the grace of God, has been rid of heretical depravity, or of Gentile superstition, or of Jewish faithlessness, or of brotherly schism, must needs come to the Church, and show a true colour of faith like to that of others.

*But one.* And the one who returned signifies the devout humility in Christ of the one Church, who, falling at his feet and giving thanks, because with the thoughts of presumption repressed he sees how weak he is, ascribes nothing of virtue to himself; the good things which he does he understands to be of mercy.

*And he fell on his face.* He falls on his face who blushes for the evils he has committed. For a man falls there where he is put to confusion. He who falls on his face sees whither he falls; he who falls backward does not see. The good therefore fall on their face, because they humble themselves in these visible things, that they may be raised to the invisible; the evil fall backward, because they fall among invisible things, where they do not see what follows them.

*Arise.* He who, acknowledging his own weakness, has lain humbly before God, is bidden by divine consolation to rise to stronger works, and to go on increasing as far as things more perfect. *Thy faith.* The faith which inclined him to give thanks; on the contrary, faithlessness condemns those who are ungrateful for benefits received. *Hath made thee whole.* In the parable above it is determined that faith ought to be increased through humility. In this one it is manifestly shown by the facts themselves, that it is not the acknowledged reason of faith only, but the executed working of faith, that makes the believer whole.

hymns.title: Father, we thank you for you planted
Praise and thanksgiving be to God our maker
Guide me, O thou great Jehovah
Mountains are all aglow with autumn colors so bright

echoes.text: There is one who scatters, and increases yet more. There is one who withholds more than is appropriate, but gains poverty. The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself. People curse someone who withholds grain, but blessing will be on the head of him who sells it.
echoes.note: Paul's maxim that sparing sowing yields sparing reaping while bountiful sowing yields bountiful reaping closely tracks the wisdom paradox 'one gives freely, yet grows all the richer; another withholds what he should give, and only suffers want.' Coherence is strong since both texts treat almsgiving under an agricultural-recompense logic, and the bountiful-eye blessing of 22:9 reinforces availability. Volume is high at the conceptual level even though Paul does not quote verbatim.

echoes.text: He who sows wickedness reaps trouble, and the rod of his fury will be destroyed. He who has a generous eye will be blessed; for he shares his food with the poor.
echoes.note: The sowing-and-reaping figure plus the 'bountiful eye' that is blessed for giving bread to the poor (22:8-9) supplies both halves of Paul's argument here and into v.7. The LXX expansion of 22:8 ('God blesses a cheerful man and a giver') is the most probable direct source of 'God loves a cheerful giver,' giving high recurrence and coherence across vv.6-7. Availability is secure since Paul cites Proverbs elsewhere.
echoes.lxxText: He that sows wickedness shall reap troubles; and shall fully receive the punishment of his deeds. God loves a cheerful and liberal man; but a man shall fully prove the folly of his works. He that has pity on the poor shall himself be maintained; for he has given of his own bread to the poor. He that gives liberally secures victory an honour; but he takes away the life of them that posses them.

echoes.text: He who sows wickedness reaps trouble, and the rod of his fury will be destroyed.
echoes.note: The clause 'God loves a cheerful giver' has no Hebrew counterpart but matches the Septuagintal plus to Proverbs 22:8b, 'God blesses a cheerful man and a giver,' nearly word for word in vocabulary (hilaron, didonta/doten). The verbal volume is high enough that most commentators treat this as Paul's source rather than free composition. The shift from 'blesses' to 'loves' is the only material variation.
echoes.lxxText: He that sows wickedness shall reap troubles; and shall fully receive the punishment of his deeds. God loves a cheerful and liberal man; but a man shall fully prove the folly of his works.

echoes.text: You shall surely give, and your heart shall not be grieved when you give to him; because that for this thing Yahweh your God will bless you in all your work, and in all that you put your hand to.
echoes.note: Paul's prohibition of giving 'grudgingly or under compulsion' echoes the Deuteronomic command to give to the poor 'and your heart shall not be grudging when you give,' with the promise that the LORD will bless you for it. Coherence is strong because both texts attach divine favor to ungrudging almsgiving. Volume is moderate; the shared idea of the un-grudging heart is distinctive enough to exceed a commonplace.

echoes.text: Glorify the Lord with a good eye, And stint not the first fruits of your hands. In every gift show a cheerful countenance, And dedicate your tithe with gladness. Give to the Most High according as he has given; And as your hand has found, give with a good eye. For the Lord recompenses, And he will recompense you sevenfold.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's instruction to glorify the Lord with a generous gift, give 'with a cheerful eye/face,' and not to be sparing because the Lord repays is a strikingly close Second-Temple parallel to Paul's cheerful, ungrudging giver. Availability and coherence are high; recurrence is supported by Sirach's wider almsgiving theology. Marked medium since Paul's nearer verbal source remains Proverbs 22:8 LXX.

echoes.text: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.
echoes.note: The prophetic summons to 'sow for yourselves righteousness, reap steadfast love' supplies the moralized sowing/reaping pattern Paul deploys, where the harvest is a moral-spiritual yield, not mere produce. Coherence is strong with v.10's 'fruits of your righteousness,' and recurrence within the chapter strengthens the case. Volume is moderate because Hosea's specific righteousness/mercy pairing surfaces more explicitly at v.10.

echoes.text: According to what I have seen, those who plow iniquity, and sow trouble, reap the same.
echoes.note: Eliphaz's observation that 'those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same' is the negative form of Paul's reciprocity principle. The connection is thematic rather than verbal, and the moral valence is inverted (Job warns of bad harvests), so volume and coherence are limited. Included as a maximal flag for the broader OT sowing-reaping topos.

echoes.text: My son, sow not upon the furrows of unrighteousness, And you shall not reap them sevenfold.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's 'do not sow in the furrows of injustice, lest you reap them sevenfold' offers a Second-Temple instance of the sowing-reaping recompense Paul assumes. Availability is good but the volume is faint and the link conceptual, since Sirach frames the negative (injustice) while Paul frames generosity positively. Marked contested as background topos rather than source.

echoes.text: He has dispersed, he has given to the poor. His righteousness endures forever. His horn will be exalted with honor.
echoes.note: Paul introduces with the formula 'as it is written' and cites Psalm 112:9 (LXX 111:9) verbatim: 'He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.' The verbal volume is maximal and the citation explicit, the clearest OT quotation in the chapter. Coherence is strong: the psalm's generous, God-fearing man models the Corinthians' almsgiving, and 'his righteousness' bridges to v.10's harvest of righteousness.

echoes.text: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater;
echoes.note: Paul's description of God as the one 'who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food' draws directly on Isaiah's image of rain that gives 'seed to the sower and bread to the eater,' the only OT verse pairing both phrases. Volume is high through the doubled, distinctive word-pair, and coherence is strong since Isaiah's seed/word fruitfulness underlies Paul's promise that God will multiply the seed. Availability is secure given Paul's heavy use of Isaiah 40-66.

echoes.text: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.
echoes.note: The promise to 'increase the fruits of your righteousness' reprises Hosea's 'sow righteousness, reap steadfast love,' where righteousness is precisely the crop. Coherence is strong because Paul fuses the agricultural supply of v.10 with a moral harvest, exactly Hosea's move. Volume is moderate; the phrase 'fruit/harvest of righteousness' is a shared idiom rather than a quotation.

echoes.text: The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life. He who is wise wins souls.
echoes.note: Paul's 'fruits of your righteousness' resonates with the wisdom maxim 'the fruit of the righteous is a tree of life,' part of the same sapiential harvest imagery. The link is idiomatic and faint relative to Hosea 10:12, so volume is low and the source contested. Flagged for completeness within the righteousness-as-fruit cluster.

echoes.text: He causes the grass to grow for the livestock, and plants for man to cultivate, that he may produce food out of the earth: wine that makes glad the heart of man, oil to make his face to shine, and bread that strengthens man’s heart.
echoes.note: God's supplying 'bread for food' (v.10) coheres with the creation psalm's praise of the LORD who brings forth 'food from the earth' and 'bread to strengthen the heart of man.' The thematic overlap of divine provision of bread is real but generic, so volume is faint and the connection contested. Isaiah 55:10 remains the stronger candidate.

echoes.text: You shall surely give, and your heart shall not be grieved when you give to him; because that for this thing Yahweh your God will bless you in all your work, and in all that you put your hand to.
echoes.note: Paul's assurance that the cheerful giver is 'enriched in everything to all liberality' echoes the Deuteronomic promise that the LORD 'will bless you in all your work' because you give to the poor. Coherence with the chapter's almsgiving theology is good, but the verbal contact is slight, so volume is low. Marked contested as a continuation of the v.7 Deuteronomy stratum.

echoes.text: The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself.
echoes.note: The sapiential principle that 'the liberal soul shall be made fat, and he who waters will himself be watered' parallels Paul's promise that giving leads to being 'enriched in everything.' The reciprocal-blessing logic matches, but the link is conceptual and contested rather than verbal. Included as a maximal flag in the generosity-enrichment cluster.

echoes.text: to appoint to those who mourn in Zion, to give to them a garland for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they may be called trees of righteousness, the planting of Yahweh, that he may be glorified.
echoes.note: Paul's repeated 'thanksgivings to God' and the people's glorifying God for the gift resonate with Isaiah's vision of the redeemed bringing praise and being called 'oaks of righteousness... that he may be glorified.' The link is thematic (almsgiving issuing in doxology) rather than verbal, so volume is faint. Flagged because Isaiah supplies the broader glory-and-righteousness horizon of the chapter.

echoes.text: Give to the Most High according as he has given; And as your hand has found, give with a good eye. For the Lord recompenses, And he will recompense you sevenfold.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's counsel that giving to the Lord is repaid sevenfold and met with a glad face stands behind Paul's claim that the saints' service overflows in 'many givings of thanks to God.' The almsgiving-thanksgiving circuit is a shared Second-Temple pattern, but the contact is conceptual, hence low volume and contested. Reinforces the Sirach stratum already noted at v.7.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: Tobit's almsgiving instruction, that giving lays up a good treasure and delivers, supplies a Second-Temple almsgiving theology congruent with Paul's account of the collection as a God-glorifying ministry. The connection is to the wider piety rather than any phrase, so volume is faint and the source contested. Included to map the deuterocanonical background of the collection ethic.

echoes.text: Please take the gift that I brought to you, because God has dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough.” He urged him, and he took it.
echoes.note: Paul's climactic 'thanks be to God for his indescribable gift' may extend the eulogia/gift register of the chapter, but no specific OT text underlies the doxology; the divine gift transcends OT precedent by design. The link to Genesis 33:11 is offered only as the chapter-spanning gift idiom. Very low volume; clearly contested.

echoes.text: Now Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honorable, because by him Yahweh had given victory to Syria: he was also a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper. The Syrians had gone out in bands, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maiden; and she waited on Naaman’s wife. She said to her mistress, “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would heal him […]
echoes.note: The Naaman narrative — a leprous Syrian foreigner cleansed who returns to the prophet to confess the God of Israel — is the structural template for the lone Samaritan leper who turns back to give thanks. The distinctive convergence of foreigner + leprosy + cleansing + grateful return gives strong Volume and Coherence, and Luke elsewhere cites Naaman explicitly (4:27), confirming Recurrence.

echoes.text: “The leper in whom the plague is shall wear torn clothes, and the hair of his head shall hang loose. He shall cover his upper lip, and shall cry, ‘Unclean! Unclean!’ All the days in which the plague is in him he shall be unclean. He is unclean. He shall dwell alone. Outside of the camp shall be his dwelling.
echoes.note: The leprosy law requires the unclean to dwell apart and cry out, explaining why the ten 'stood at a distance' and lifted their voices. The pericope presupposes this purity legislation as its narrative grammar, giving high Coherence and Availability.

echoes.text: “This shall be the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing. He shall be brought to the priest, and the priest shall go out of the camp. The priest shall examine him, and behold, if the plague of leprosy is healed in the leper, then the priest shall command them to take for him who is to be cleansed two living clean birds, and cedar wood, and scarlet, and hyssop.
echoes.note: The cleansed leper must be presented to the priest for inspection and rites of restoration, exactly what Jesus commands: 'Go, show yourselves to the priests.' The direct dependence on the priestly examination law gives high Volume and Coherence.

echoes.text: The cloud departed from over the Tent; and behold, Miriam was leprous, as white as snow. Aaron looked at Miriam, and behold, she was leprous. Aaron said to Moses, “Oh, my lord, please don’t count this sin against us, in which we have done foolishly, and in which we have sinned. Let her not, I pray, be as one dead, of whom the flesh is half consumed when he comes out of his mother’s womb.” Moses cried to Yahweh, saying, “Heal her, God, I beg you!” Yahweh […]
echoes.note: Miriam's leprosy, exclusion 'outside the camp' for seven days, and restoration by intercession reinforce the segregation-and-cleansing pattern shaping the leper episode. Moderate Coherence; the motif overlaps with the Leviticus laws, so it adds recurrence rather than independent Volume.

echoes.text: Now there were four leprous men at the entrance of the gate. They said one to another, “Why do we sit here until we die?
echoes.note: The four lepers at the gate of Samaria who 'stood at the entrance' likewise embody the marginalized-leper-at-a-distance topos and the Samaria setting. Geographic and situational resonance, but no verbal dependence, so low.

echoes.text: Praise Yahweh, my soul! All that is within me, praise his holy name! Praise Yahweh, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits; who forgives all your sins; who heals all your diseases;
echoes.note: The psalm's call to 'bless the Lord, O my soul... who heals all your diseases' coheres with the Samaritan's loud-voiced glorifying of God for his healing. Thematic only; faint.

registers.label: Spare
lines: You crown the year with your bounty; the valleys deck themselves with grain.
The earth is full of the goodness of God.
Ten were healed; one came back to say thank you.
We return to give God thanks and praise.
Remember the Lord your God, who brought you into a good land.
We will not forget the hand that feeds us.
Come, let us worship the Giver of every good gift.
We come with grateful hearts. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Look out over the fields at harvest, the valleys clothed with grain, the wagon tracks running over with abundance — God has visited the earth and watered it.
The earth is full of the goodness of God.
We come like the one leper who turned back, who fell at Jesus' feet and could not stop saying thank you.
The earth is full of the goodness of God.
Remember the bread in the wilderness, the springs in the dry land, the good country God has given us to keep.
The earth is full of the goodness of God.
And do not say, my own hand has won me this; every harvest is a gift, every breath is grace.
The earth is full of the goodness of God.
So come with full hands and fuller hearts, and give God thanks.
The earth is full of the goodness of God. Thanks be to God!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: You crown the year with bounty; the fields are decked with grain.
The earth is full of God's goodness.
One leper turned back to say thank you.
The earth is full of God's goodness.
Remember the Lord who brings us into a good land.
The earth is full of God's goodness.
Come, let us worship the Giver of all gifts.
We come with grateful hearts. Amen.
